T3A01: At VHF, signals reflect off buildings, hills, and vehicles and reach your antenna by multiple paths. Depending on exact position, the reflected waves either add together (reinforce) or cancel out. So moving a few feet, which is about a wavelength at VHF, can change signal strength dramatically.
T3A02: Leaves and trees contain water, which absorbs UHF and microwave energy. Foliage can greatly weaken signals, especially weak ones, which is why microwave links need a clear path.
T3A03: Long-distance (weak-signal) CW and SSB on VHF/UHF normally uses horizontal polarization. FM and repeaters normally use vertical polarization. Using the same polarization as the other station matters at VHF/UHF.
T3A04: Cross-polarization means one station is vertical and the other horizontal. On a direct line-of-sight path, this causes a large reduction in received signal strength, often 20 dB or more.
T3A05: If the direct path is blocked, aim your directional antenna to bounce your signal off a building, hill, or other reflector so that it reaches the repeater. 'Long path' is an HF concept and doesn't apply here.
T3A06: 'Picket fencing' is the rapid fluttering of a mobile signal caused by multipath as the vehicle moves through areas where reflections add and cancel. It sounds like a stick dragged along a picket fence.
T3A07: At microwave frequencies, rain, snow, and other precipitation absorb and scatter signals, reducing range. Wind, pressure, and temperature have little direct effect.
T3A08: Signals arriving via the ionosphere often take several paths, which keep changing. They combine randomly, adding or canceling, causing irregular fading (QSB).
T3A09: Signals coming back from the ionosphere have random, elliptical polarization. As a result, either a vertical or horizontal antenna will work for HF sky-wave contacts. Matching polarization doesn't matter the way it does at VHF line-of-sight.
T3A10: Multipath causes copies of the data signal to arrive at slightly different times, smearing the symbols together. This makes the receiver more likely to misread them, so error rates increase.
T3A11: The ionosphere (roughly 50-400 km up) contains ionized layers that refract HF radio waves back to Earth. This is what makes long-distance HF 'skip' contacts possible.
T3A12: At HF and low VHF (10 and 6 meters), the wavelength is long compared to raindrops, so fog and rain have little effect. Rain becomes a problem mainly at microwave frequencies.
T3B01: In an electromagnetic wave, the electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular (at right angles) to each other, and both are perpendicular to the direction the wave travels.
T3B02: Polarization is defined by the orientation of the electric field. A vertical antenna produces a vertical electric field, giving vertical polarization.
T3B03: A radio wave consists of an electric field and a magnetic field oscillating together. Voltage and current exist in the antenna and wires, not in the wave itself.
T3B04: In free space, radio waves travel at the speed of light, because they are electromagnetic waves, the same as light. That's about 300,000,000 meters per second.
T3B05: Wavelength and frequency are inversely related: as frequency increases, wavelength gets shorter. That's why the 2-meter band (146 MHz) has a shorter wavelength than the 10-meter band (28 MHz).
T3B06: Wavelength in meters = 300 / frequency in MHz. Example: 300 / 146 MHz ≈ 2 meters. The 300 comes from the speed of light (300,000,000 m/s) with the 'millions' canceling out.
T3B07: Amateur bands are commonly identified by their approximate wavelength in meters, such as '2 meters' for 144-148 MHz or '70 centimeters' for 420-450 MHz.
T3B08: VHF (Very High Frequency) is 30 to 300 MHz. This includes the 6-meter, 2-meter, and 1.25-meter amateur bands.
T3B09: UHF (Ultra High Frequency) is 300 to 3000 MHz. This includes the 70 cm, 33 cm, and 23 cm amateur bands.
T3B10: HF (High Frequency) is 3 to 30 MHz. The 'shortwave' bands from 80 meters through 10 meters fall in HF. Note that 160 meters (1.8 MHz) is technically MF.
T3B11: Radio waves travel at about 300,000,000 meters per second in free space, the speed of light. Note the units: meters per second, not miles per hour.
T3B12: All electromagnetic waves, regardless of frequency, travel at the same speed in free space: the speed of light. Frequency changes only the wavelength, not the speed.
T3C01: UHF signals normally pass right through the ionosphere instead of being refracted back to Earth. So without ionospheric skip, UHF simplex is limited to about line-of-sight plus a bit (the radio horizon).
T3C02: HF is where long-distance ionospheric (sky-wave) propagation is common. VHF and higher only occasionally get ionospheric propagation. HF antennas are larger, and HF has more static, not less.
T3C03: Signals reflected off the aurora are distorted, with a raspy, buzzing sound, because the aurora is constantly moving. Stations usually point their antennas north toward the aurora.
T3C04: Sporadic E occurs when patches of the E region become strongly ionized, briefly reflecting 10, 6, and sometimes 2 meter signals hundreds to over a thousand miles. It's especially common in late spring and summer.
T3C05: Knife-edge diffraction occurs when radio waves bend around a sharp edge, such as a mountain ridge or a building's edge, allowing signals to reach the area behind the obstruction.
T3C06: Tropospheric ducting traps VHF/UHF signals in a layer of the lower atmosphere, carrying them about 300 miles or more beyond the normal horizon. It happens regularly in some areas, especially along coastlines.
T3C07: 6 meters is the best band for meteor scatter, because the ionized trails left by meteors reflect lower VHF frequencies best. Meteor scatter contacts last just seconds, so fast digital modes (such as MSK144) are often used.
T3C08: Tropospheric ducting is caused by temperature inversions, where a layer of warm air sits above cooler air. The inversion bends radio waves back toward Earth, forming a duct.
T3C09: 10-meter F-region propagation is best during daylight (dawn to shortly after sunset) and during periods of high sunspot activity, when the ionosphere is strongly ionized enough to refract 28 MHz signals.
T3C10: At the peak of the sunspot cycle, the F region can become ionized enough to reflect signals as high as 6 meters (50 MHz), and 10 meters is often wide open. UHF bands never use F-region skip.
T3C11: The atmosphere bends (refracts) radio waves slightly back toward Earth, so the radio horizon is about 15% farther than the visual horizon. Radio waves don't travel faster than light.
T4A01: Mobile radios run on 13.8 V (a car's nominal voltage while running). A 50-watt FM radio draws roughly 10 amps or more when transmitting, so a supply rated at 13.8 V and 12 A is appropriate. 4 A is too little current.
T4A02: SWR meters are designed for specific frequency ranges and power levels. Choose one rated for the band(s) and power you'll use, or the readings will be inaccurate (and the meter may be damaged).
T4A03: When transmitting, the radio draws a lot of current, and thin or long wires have resistance that causes a voltage drop (V = I × R). Short, heavy-gauge wire keeps the voltage at the radio high enough to work properly.
T4A04: For FT8 and similar sound-card digital modes, the radio's audio output goes to the computer's audio input, and the computer's audio output goes to the radio's audio input. The FT8 software (such as WSJT-X) does the encoding and decoding.
T4A05: An RF power meter must be inserted in the feed line between the transmitter and the antenna, so the RF energy passes through it.
T4A06: A computer-radio interface carries receive audio (radio to computer), transmit audio (computer to radio), and transmitter keying (PTT), so the computer can switch the radio into transmit.
T4A07: One required connection: the computer's 'line in' (audio input) is connected to the radio's speaker or audio output, so the computer can hear and decode received signals. 'Line out' to the speaker would be backwards.
T4A08: Flat copper strap is preferred for RF bonding because it has low inductance at radio frequencies (RF current flows on the surface, and a wide strap has lots of surface). Coax braid can corrode and isn't as effective.
T4A09: Battery runtime (hours) = ampere-hour rating ÷ average current draw. For example, a 20 Ah battery powering equipment that averages 2 A will last about 10 hours.
T4A10: A hotspot is a small low-power device that connects your digital voice radio (DMR, D-STAR, Fusion, etc.) to the internet-linked digital network, giving you network access even without a nearby digital repeater.
T4A11: Connect the mobile radio's negative lead directly at the battery's chassis ground connection. This gives a solid, low-resistance return and reduces noise. Random metal parts of the car may have poor connections.
T4A12: An electronic keyer helps you send Morse code manually. Used with a paddle, it automatically generates correctly timed dots and dashes.
T4B01: Too much microphone gain on SSB overdrives the transmitter, resulting in distorted transmitted audio (and possibly splatter onto adjacent frequencies).
T4B02: You set the operating frequency using the radio's keypad (direct entry) or by turning the VFO (Variable Frequency Oscillator) tuning knob. CTCSS and DTMF are tone signaling functions, not frequency controls.
T4B03: To hear a weak FM signal, set the squelch so the audio is open all the time (squelch fully off or very low). A weak signal may not be strong enough to open the squelch otherwise.
T4B04: An FM receiver tuned slightly off frequency produces distorted audio. Unlike SSB, the pitch does not change.
T4B05: The scan function automatically steps through a range of frequencies or memory channels and stops when it finds activity.
T4B06: RIT (Receiver Incremental Tuning), also called a 'clarifier,' lets you adjust the receive frequency slightly without changing your transmit frequency. On SSB, a signal off frequency sounds high or low-pitched, so RIT fixes that.
T4B07: A DMR code plug is the configuration file loaded into your radio. It contains frequencies, color codes, talkgroups, and contacts. It's how you program a DMR radio.
T4B08: Choosing a filter bandwidth that matches the mode (for example, narrow for CW, ~2.4 kHz for SSB) cuts out noise and interfering signals outside the desired signal.
T4B09: On DMR, you select a group of stations (a talkgroup) by entering or selecting its identification code. Talkgroup IDs are normally stored in your code plug.
T4B10: An SSB voice signal is about 2.4 kHz wide, so a 2400 Hz filter passes the whole signal while rejecting noise outside it. Narrower filters cut off voice; wider filters let in extra noise.
T4B11: D-STAR radios transmit your call sign digitally with every transmission, so you must program your call sign into the radio before transmitting.
